doc.title: Benny Golson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Return to New York and Europe
title: Setting goals for Blakey's band, then the All-Star Messengers reunions
summary: Golson recalls getting Small's Paradise to ask for Blakey again and describes joining the All-Star Jazz Messengers tours in 1983 and 1989.

bands.name: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: So you resume off and on in various configurations the Jazztet, but you also get back with Art Blakey again, who you helped to get on the track. You did several reunions.

He stayed on the track, too. He really did. The money stayed up. He presented the group in a good way. He learned how – when to take the intermission, to come back. It was so messed up before. When he was playing Small’s Paradise before I joined him, he would play – an intermission was 20 minutes, and he would be gone an hour, an hour and a half. They said they never wanted him back in there again. So when I took the group over, I said, “We have to set goals for ourselves. One of the goals – one of the first goals is going to be that Small’s Paradise asks for this group.” He said, “Oh, no. It’ll never happen,” because he had messed up so bad. We got the group together, got our repertoire together, recorded. Bobby Timmons, I got him to finish that tune he thought was no good, Moanin’. Blue March, CD – 45 came. It was on all the jukeboxes in Harlem, Moanin’. Ring. “This is Small’s Paradise. Is Art Blakey available?” He says, “I don’t believe it.” I said, “That tells you we’re moving in the right direction.” Because you have to set goals for yourself, to know where you’re going, landmarks.

According to this chronology, you were with Art Blakey again in ’83 and then again in ’89. He passed in ’90. What was it like coming back, working with Art Blakey? He still had that same fire, that same magic?

Coming back to a drummer swinging like that was like paradise. It’s like going to get another gourmet meal. That was – when I came back, it was as the All-Star Jazz Messengers: his current group, plus Jackie McLean, Curtis, and me. That’s what that was, those tours. It wasn’t just the regular group. The last time we did it, I think it was Terence Blanchard and Donald Harrison. They were in the group then.
